The earliest life stages of Dover sole Microstomus pacificus are characterised by a remarkably brief egg and larval period at the cold temperatures typical of their Northeast Pacific benthic habitat. Eggs released during broadcast spawning and fertilised externally develop into yolk-dependent embryos that undergo eclosion after approximately 41 days [ab = approximately 41 days] when incubated at a stable 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C]. The newly emerged prolarvae are lecithotrophic and possess a prominent yolk sac, measuring just 0.0011 grams [Wwb = 0.0011 grams] in wet weight at birth, a value consistent with the small egg diameters reported for the related species Microstomus kitt. This minimal initial mass reflects the substantial constraints imposed by cold-water incubation, where smaller eggs are advantageous for gas exchange during the prolonged incubation period. The larvae remain non-feeding for a brief interval following chorion rupture, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves as they initiate the gradual process of yolk absorption. The environmental conditions at 3.5 °C are thus a critical determinant of early developmental success.

Following the completion of yolk-sac resorption and the onset of exogenous feeding, the free-swimming larvae of Microstomus pacificus enter a protracted pelagic larval phase characterised by active growth in the water column. Field surveys indicate that individuals eventually attain a total length at puberty of 38.5 centimeters [Lp = 38.5 centimeters], a size that marks the transition from the immature post-metamorphic juvenile stage to reproductive viability. This pubertal length is reached after a period of substantial somatic investment, during which the growing juveniles shift from a planktonic diet to benthic prey items following larval metamorphosis and settlement. The corresponding wet weight at puberty of 476 grams [Wwp = 476 grams] has been estimated from morphometric relationships and is typical for a pleuronectiform of this body plan. Achieving this mass requires the efficient conversion of ingested resources into axial muscle and visceral tissue, a process influenced by the seasonal availability of polychaetes and small crustaceans on the continental shelf.

The maximum reproductive output of female Dover sole has been characterised under controlled laboratory conditions that mimic the thermal regime of their primary spawning grounds. At a stable environmental temperature of 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C], a single female can produce approximately 630 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 630 eggs per spawning event] across the peak of the spawning season, with an average of one continuous spawning event each year [F_R_i = one continuous spawning event each year]. These values reflect a reproductive strategy that prioritises a moderate per-spawning fecundity sustained over a prolonged interval rather than a massive single pulse of gametes. The annual output is thus considerable when integrated across the entire reproductive window. This per-event fecundity, taken together with the annual spawning frequency, indicates that reproductive effort in this species is heavily influenced by the energetic reserves accumulated during the preceding feeding season.

Growth in length continues throughout the lifespan of Microstomus pacificus, though the rate of increase slows markedly after the onset of sexual maturation. The largest individuals recorded in commercial trawl surveys and scientific sampling programmes achieve an ultimate total length of 76 centimeters [Li = 76 centimeters], a size that represents the asymptotic maximum for the species. Adult females at this length attain an ultimate wet weight of 3800 grams [Wwi = 3800 grams], a mass that is approximately eight times greater than the mass at puberty. This considerable post-pubertal growth is possible because Dover sole are iteroparous and continue to allocate resources to somatic tissue even while investing in annual reproductive events. The length-weight relationship used to derive this maximal mass follows a standard power function common among flatfishes, reflecting isometric scaling of body depth with length.

Longevity records for Dover sole indicate a remarkably extended lifespan relative to many other northeast Pacific flatfishes, with the oldest documented individuals persisting for approximately 60 years [am = approximately 60 years] under the cold, low-metabolic conditions of their 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C] habitat. This extreme longevity is made possible by a slow pace of life that delays senescence and allows for repeated spawning events across many decades. The age at birth of 41 days [ab = 41 days] following fertilisation is a brief period in the context of a lifespan that can span six decades at a temperature of 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C]. Such a life-history strategy, combining a minuscule birth mass, a moderate size at puberty, and a very late age at death, places Microstomus pacificus among the slower end of the teleost life-history continuum, a position likely reinforced by the consistently low temperatures of its deep-water environment.
